The chief of their office in Pristina, Beatrice Weber, was informed of all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this part of their activities or did it go beyond their official activities?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, this went beyond their sphere of activity, which is why this document was compiled and forwarded to the ministry. And then through other ministries appropriate steps could be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this report go through your line of work?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I seem to have omitted something in the case of document 6D262, so could we have it back on the screen, please. We have again before us a document issued by the Ministry of the Interior on the 18th of June, 1998. Is this dispatch of an instructory [as interpreted] nature?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It says how employees of the police should behave and how they should conduct themselves with respect to representatives of international organizations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And at the end of the document on page 3 it's signed by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. Could the minister issue such instructory dispatches to you along your line of work?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the minister could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in Kosovo and Metohija as a member of the staff, were you within the line of management in the administration for foreign nationals [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: While I was engaged in these tasks, I was not in the line of management of the border police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did the border police stations inform you of anything; and if so, what did they inform you about?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I received daily reports from the border police stations about the flow of passengers on the border posts and the same reports were sent to the border police administration. So these reports were sent to me for information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if there's a difficulty in the transcript, the border police administration sprang from nowhere, 46, 11 and 12, were you in the line of management in the -- now, what was your question, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll clarify that with the witness rather than me testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the administration which was in charge of the border police stations and where was it located?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: This administration was called the border police administration, and its headquarters was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the part of the Novi Sad SUP from which you went to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: That was the border police department for foreign nationals, passports, and weapons. If I may clarify. As it's a long name, we used an abbreviated form of the name. So the administration was referred to as the border police administration and the departments were called either the department for foreign nationals or the department of border police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the border police administration and your department of border police in the Novi Sad SUP and the border police station, were they all in the same line of work in the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: We all belonged to the same line of work, but the border police department belonged to the Novi Sad SUP, whereas the border police stations belonged directly to the border police administration and they belonged directly to it. So that the border police department did not have any authority over the border police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Novi Sad is in Vojvodina. While you were working in the border police department in Novi Sad, did your department in Novi Sad have any powers or authority over the border police stations in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The department I worked in had no authority over the border police stations in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the MUP staff along that line of work, apart from you, was there anybody else?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: In the MUP of the Republic of Serbia [as interpreted], there was no one else, apart from me, dealing with that line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think you described it, but to clarify for the record let me ask you the following. As a member of the staff could you issue binding orders to the border police stations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, I could not issue binding orders to the border police stations. That was done by the administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is another I think inaccuracy there. You were asked in the MUP staff, apart from you, was there anyone else in that line of work. And your answer was: "There was no one else, apart from me, dealing with that line of work in the MUP of the Republic of Serbia." Now, did you mean to state your unique position so broadly as that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably the interpreters misunderstood me. I said in the staff of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this isn't confined to the staff in Pristina or in Novi Sad, this is -- you are the only one in the MUP dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand your question. Could you repeat it, please, or make it shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you understand my confusion, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you assist, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- Serbian is clear. I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you assist, then please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just give us the name of the body where you were the only member dealing with that line of work.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: That was the staff of the Ministry of the Interior. I was the only one there dealing with that line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In what place was the staff you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The staff was in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What then was your role in the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have already stated, my fundamental role consisted in contacts with representatives of international organizations. As I have already said, I received reports from the border police stations and informed the staff leader or manager of any security-related events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to your work in both parts of the Ministry of the Interior, in the state security where, if I understand you correctly, you worked for only a year. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, only a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that within the Ministry of the Interior one side might issue binding orders to the other side?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, that was not possible. These were two entirely separate organizational units of the Ministry of the Interior. The only thing they had in common was the minister of the interior, who was superior to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did these two sectors cooperate; and if so, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, these two sectors did cooperate in terms of exchanging information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already told us about the line of work of the border police stations, and you told us that they received their orders, "nalog," from the administration for border affairs. What was the relationship like between the border police stations in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999 with the SUPs on whose territory they were?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Kosovo and Metohija the organization was the same like throughout the territory of the Republic of Serbia, that is to say that all border police stations, not only in Kosovo and Metohija but in the other parts of the Republic of Serbia as well, are directly linked to the administration of the border police. Territorially, they are in the area of a secretariat of the interior, but they are independent organizational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the role of the departments for border affairs or foreign nationals within the respective SUPs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The departments of border police dealt with status-related questions pertaining to foreign nationals, then the issuance of passports to the citizens of the Republic of Serbia, then the issuing of personal identity cards, then questions related to weapons, issuing weapons permits, and registering weapons. Also questions related to nationality in the sense of statehood and other such affairs. There was a broad range of work that these divisions and departments carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That cannot be seen from this abbreviated name, but if we look at the full name of these departments we see that they are in charge of all of these affairs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember now, we didn't really work on this, what the full name of these departments is?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: It changed several times, but I think it's the department of the border police for foreign nationals, passports or travel documents, and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also for administrative matters, because you did refer to personal identity cards as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for administrative matters too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who headed the border police administration in 1998 and 1999, so the administration in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 in the administration there was no chief of the administration, there was an active -- acting chief. So it was a deputy chief who was acting chief, and that was Mr. Petar Dujkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who adopts the documents regulating the work of the border police administration?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned, this administration uses many regulations, the bylaws are adopted by the minister, such as the rules and instructions involved. Lower-ranking documents, like instructive dispatches and orders, "nalog," are adopted by the chief of the administration or the chief of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the transcript is not very clear. These instructions and orders, "nalog," were they adopted or passed by the chief of the administration or the chief of the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, the instructive dispatches, this is a term that is used, are adopted or passed by the chief of the administration. However, if this deals with a more important question, as we've already seen, then it can be done by the chief of section himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It wasn't that I was not satisfied with your answer. We just needed to clarify something for the sake of the record. Were organizational units duty-bound to adopt plans of work?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Plans -- organs -- all organizational units pass an annual and monthly plan of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The MUP staff in Kosovo, while you were its member, did it ever pass an organizational plan for any MUP unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such thing. As for my line of work, and I don't think that this was not done and I did not see it done for any other line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What regulation regulates information and reporting within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: May I answer? This field is regulated by the instruction on information and reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Types of information in this instruction?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: According to this information, there is urgent information and regular information. Regular information involves the writing of daily bulletins of events, monthly reports on work, and annual reports on work. Sometimes biannual and trimesteral reports are written as well. It depends on what the urgent matters are going to be that the ministry should be informed of, that is to say that every organizational unit knows what it is about which it has to be -- it has to send an urgent report to the administration within the ministry that is involved for such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since this document is not translated, I need to say for the sake of the record that we need to look at 6D1323. Mr. Vucurevic, I would like to ask you something else now, what was the role of the staff and what was your personal role in daily reporting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Every day from all the secretariats of the interior in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija we received reports about the state of security in their respective areas. These reports were reviewed by us and we also wrote a report that we sent to the Ministry of the Interior. However, I wish to point out that these secretariats along parallel lines sent these same reports to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Within the staff was this information analysed, this information that was received from the SUPs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Analytical processing did take place, as far as I know, since the ministry received the same reports only the most important events would be included in these reports, that is to say major crimes, terrorist attacks, and terrorist provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you personally, what kind of data did you receive and did you bring together some reports or some data that you received?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: When the Kosovo Verification Mission was established, the staff did receive reports about which police employees had contacts with the Kosovo Verification Mission. These reports arrived in the staff, and then we would write an aggregated report and then we would send it to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us just go back to the reports that you received from the border police stations. What was the nature of these reports that you got from them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: These are regular reports that are written by all border police stations, that is to say about the exit and entry into the country, the number of persons involved in that, how many vehicles went out and came in to the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is: Were these statistical reports or did they go beyond that, the ones that you received regularly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: These were statistical reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What legal regulations did you apply during the course of your work, if you can remember now?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that we did indeed use many laws, first of all, the Law on the Personal Identity Card, then the Law on Domicile and Residence, the Law on Travel Documents, the Law on Citizenship, then the Law on the Movement and Stay of Citizens -- Foreign Citizens, then the Law on Weapons and Ammunition, the Law on Crossing the State Border and Movement in the Border Area, then the Law on Associations of Citizens, and I think that I have enumerated all of them. Perhaps I omitted some.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That will do. Thank you. Now I would like to call up in e-court a Prosecution document, P1505. Mr. Vucurevic, you have before you a decision on the establishment of the staff of the ministry dated the 16th of June, 1998. First of all I would like to ask you the following. Before you were sent out to Kosovo and Metohija, did the MUP staff exist, the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you sent to the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija we saw that --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I received that decision on my sending there in March 1998, and I started working there on the 1st of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was head of staff then when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The head of staff then was Mr. Aco Vesovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From which administration was Mr. Vesovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vesovic worked in the administration of traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us have a look at this decision dated the 16th of June, 1998. Some persons are referred to here. Can you tell us, you can leaf through this document, can you tell us who the members of the staff were from the 16th of April -- rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- 16th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, the head of the staff was Mr. Sreten Lukic. Then Radislav Djinovic worked on the staff. I cannot remember exactly, but I think that briefly, soon after this date, that's to say the end of June, he left the staff, then Goran Radosavljevic, Novica Zdravkovic, and later on Desimir Slovic came and Dusko Adamovic. Also, there were persons there who were working at the Pristina SUP, such as Milorad Rajicic, Rasko Milenkovic, and Dr. Dobrasin Krdzic and Milutin Vukovic. I think that he also worked in the Pristina SUP. I just omitted Mr. Milan Cankovic. I don't know where exactly he worked, but I know that he was sent to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, no microphone I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see in this decision that there is a reference to some names that you had not mentioned as being the staff members. So now I'm going to ask you about them. David Gajic, was he a member of the staff after the 16th of June, 1998, or perhaps before that, too, because you were on the staff before that as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, David Gajic was not a member of the staff. When I came he wasn't and he wasn't later either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the deputy head of staff, the deputy head of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The deputy head was Mr. Miroslav Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see Milorad Lukovic being referred to as assistant head of staff. Was Milorad Lukovic a member of this staff while you were a member of this staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We also see Zivko Trajkovic referred to here. Was he a member of the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the members of the staff who were not at the same time employed with the Pristina SUP, did they have offices at the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: All of us who were sent to the staff of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia had offices there in the building of the Pristina SUP. So it was not a separate building housing the MUP staff. We were together with the other employees of the SUP Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the members of the staff who had simultaneous duties in the SUP of Pristina, where were they seated?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: They performed their regular duties in their own offices with the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you now turn to page 2. We can see that after these names listed there is a reference to an expanded composition of the staff, and it says that members of the staff in its expanded composition include heads of secretariats. Were heads of secretariats of the interior from Kosovo and Metohija indeed members of the staff and what kind of expanded composition is this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what this term, expanded staff, means, but I can tell you that chiefs of secretariats were not members of the staff and I can explain in greater detail why I don't think they were. Chiefs of secretariats of internal affairs did not come to meetings at the staff on a daily basis, nor did we have daily contact with them. I too attended some meetings, four or five, at the MUP staff of the Republic of Serbia in Pristina. They performed their regular jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this same paragraph it says that chiefs of centres and sectors, or rather, sections --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 58, line 5, if you allow me for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There must be something missing from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is something missing. The witness said that chiefs of secretariats attended those four or five meetings, whereas it seems for the record -- from the record that he was the only one who attended them. He plus the chiefs of secretariats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you happy with that interpretation, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll have to clarify it with the witness. I would rather do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were telling us about chiefs of SUPs.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, for the record, repeat your answer. How often did they come?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you, I didn't see them every day in the building which housed the staff. I saw them perhaps four or five times at the staff when some meetings were held, but those were not staff meetings. Those were meetings attended either by the minister of the interior or the chief of the public security sector or perhaps the president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic. I forgot to mention him earlier. That's why I said I thought there were not members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, were chiefs of centres and sections of state security in the area of Kosovo and Metohija members of the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not members of the staff either, as far as I know. I did not have any contact with them and I didn't see them at all. I can only add the same thing that I said about chiefs of SUPs. When some high-ranking state officials visited, they would come, but I didn't otherwise see them and I didn't even know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did members of the staff come regularly to those offices from which they worked, or almost every day?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: We came to work every day like all the other employees of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Goran Radosavljevic was in command of some units?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Not that I know. As far as I know, his work was in training. As far as I know, he graduated from the school of physical education at the university and his job was to train policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We saw that decision to send you to Kosovo and Metohija, 6D1048, and the decision terminating your engagement, which was 6D1049. So in that connection I'd like to ask you, was the head of the staff able to appoint members?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the head of staff dismiss any member of the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, he could not, because he was not the one who made decisions on appointment or termination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the MUP staff -- could the MUP staff or its head appoint or replace or recall policemen in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are still with this decision to establish the MUP staff of the 16th of June. Now, on page 2 could you please focus on paragraph marked with the Roman numeral II, in English it's not a Roman numeral, but it deals with the tasks of the staff. It says: "The staff is tasked with planning, organizing, and managing the activities and employment of the organizational units of the ministry, including the units sent and seconded and suppressing terrorism in the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija." We have discussed plans already, but I'm going to ask you again in view of this decision. Did the MUP staff plan the work of MUP organizational units in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, the MUP staff did not plan the work of organizational units in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it organize the work of these organizational units?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The staff did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who organizes the staff of organizational units?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who organizes the work of organizational units, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The chief of secretariat, the chief of SUP, that is, the secretariat for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the level of OUPs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the OUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the staff supervise the work and employment of organizational units?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, it did not supervise the work and employment of organizational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the MUP staff organize and supervise anti-terrorist actions, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the staff did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this decision to establish the staff in the period while you were on it, did it ever work in practice?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Not in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's a document that I did not announce, it's 6D798, so I'm not going to show it to you but it is a record -- the minutes of a meeting held at the staff on the 22nd of July, 1998. This document is already an exhibit in this case. I'm told that Mr. Petrovic did announce it for the cross-examination of this witness and it was also announced by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the Chamber give me leave to use it myself or shall I continue without using the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any objection to it being used?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue -- yes, you may use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you have it either, so could you please look at it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 6D798 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, do you see yourself among those who attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning the agenda of that meeting, and the problem with this document is that it is incomplete so that on the following page we have only one paragraph and we don't see everything that was done at the meeting from these minutes. But from the portion we can see I would like to ask you if the agenda included what is indicated in item 3, what is written there.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Item 3 reads: "Defining or identifying tasks connected with the implementation of the general [as interpreted] plan and the follow-up task."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of that meeting, was there, indeed, discussion about that general [as interpreted] plan and what was said?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember all the details, but from what I remember that was the first time I heard of such a plan. That plan was essentially about taking an action to suppress terrorism in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, because as far as I remember at that time many roads were blocked and normal movement along those roads was impossible. Those roads were held by members of the KLA. So it was the first time I ever heard of such a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I rise to raise an issue about translation. The translation of that paragraph 3 in court today has been "general plan" where the document says "global plan," and maybe no one else does, but I see a difference between those two terms, between "global" and "general."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Interestingly, I think the Serb word used was "global" in the question, and I was somewhat surprised at the translation and I was about to raise it. So let's ask the interpreter to consider again what is the correct translation of the expression that both Mr. Lukic and the witness used to describe the plan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is purely my opinion that the word "general" corresponds better to the actual meaning because the word "global" in English means "world." But I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a situation which I think is best dealt with following reflection, and therefore we shall invite CLSS to review this particular sentence, that's the sentence number 3 in the first page of these minutes, and we'll proceed conscious of the potential difficulty of accurately interpreting this reference. Please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this meeting we see a list of the other people who attended, they are listed here, but tell us if they were really present, General Vlastimir Djordjevic and General Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who in fact informed you of this plan and the tasks?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly now whether it was Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic or perhaps Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it was one of the two?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did one of the two tell you about that plan, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, after all this time it's difficult to remember everything that went on at a meeting, but I believe it was said that because of the very difficult situation in the area of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, the state leadership or somebody else, but I think the word state leadership was mentioned, adopted that plan to prevent terrorism. And as far as I remember, it was said that the plan would involve the participation of the units of the VJ, the Army of Yugoslavia, and police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have seen that General Djordjevic and General Stevanovic were in Kosovo and Metohija at the time. Did they stay after the meeting and until when?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, they did stay but I cannot tell you until when, until September I believe or end October. They stayed in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said until end September or end October, so when these actions were finished they left Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember after the departure of the KVM which left on the 20th of March, 1999, before the air-strikes did General Obrad Stevanovic again come to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think he did and I think he was in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I now wish to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's a suitable time, I would like to make a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to break for lunch at this stage, Mr. Vucurevic, that will be for an hour. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Arrangements have been made OLAD to enable the previous witness to have the opportunity of legal advice before answering any further questions. The lawyer who will be available for consultation with him is Jelena Nikolic, she is presently involved in matters at the UNDU and cannot be here until 1.00 at the earliest. But so that she may make use of the time available when she does arrive and before we resume, I will say now what I would have said in her presence and this can be shown to her when she does arrive, that what the Chamber wishes is that she should meet with the witness, advise him that the Chamber have assigned her as a lawyer from whom he may take advice on his rights under Rule 90(E) before continuing with his evidence. And if he indicates that he wishes advice from her, then she should provide the advice he requires. And then we would hear from her before the evidence resumes that she's satisfied that she's complied with that undertaking and that he understands the position before we continue. Now, does any counsel want to add anything that should be drawn to her attention?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I think that I just learned something from my colleagues, that she was appointed to represent Mr. Djordjevic, Vlastimir Djordjevic, for the initial appearance, duty counsel at that time. I don't know if it can raise any problems. And for Pantic, she was in Belgrade even more, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For Mr. Pantic she was present in Belgrade during his -- Momir Pantic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you see as the problem there? She does not act for Djordjevic, she did appear for his initial appearance. She's not directly involved in that case in a capacity that could cause a conflict of interest so far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In my dealings with her in connection with that brief representation, I understand she had actually very little communication with Mr. Djordjevic because I think he didn't want her. And so there wasn't a lot of substantive contact, from my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are not objecting, just to be clear just for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm more concerned to know if there's anything that should be added to what I've just indicated. I don't think it's right to be any more specific about the circumstances of the questioning. The witness is in midstream and there is no need for the details to be discussed, but it's open to him to raise with her any issues that he thinks might fall under the rule and to seek advice. It's not for us to guide any further on this I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- I think your remarks instructed her to advise him of the contents of the rule, but I'm not certain about that. I think that's probably important that she read the rule to him or let him understand the rule, because otherwise he may have no idea what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm very reluctant to try to tell my -- I've got to watch what I say here. There's a terrible English expression which I won't use. But I have to be careful not to try to tell someone her job. There are certain basic things that I think we can assume she will address, and we are dealing with an experienced attorney who will be able I think very readily to give the necessary advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Apparently she has sought more information about the circumstances. I don't want to prevent necessary disclosure, and I would be I think assisted by counsel considering any request for further information and hopefully reaching agreement on what should be provided. If she feels unhappy about dealing with the job without further information, then hopefully among counsel agreement can be reached on what further information she should be given. If there is any difficulty, then we will have to resume at 1.45 with her in court and we can deal openly with what she requires. So we'll resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.51 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we'll continue with this witness for half an hour and hope that by that time we can deal with Mr. Milenkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry for the delay, Mr. Vucurevic. Technical problems prevented us starting any quicker. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vucurevic, we will now move on to the relations between the MUP staff, although we've already spoken about this, but we'll go into it deeper, and the organizational units of the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija. So please let's have on e-court Exhibit 6D266. You have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who sent this document and who are the recipients?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: This document was sent out by the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, the public security sector, and it was addressed to the secretariats of the interior in Pristina, Kosovska Mitrovica, Pec, Djakovica, Prizren, Urosevac, Gnjilane, Vranje, Leskovac, Prokuplje, Kraljevo, and Novi Pazar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you here for a minute. Are these the secretariats of the interior in Kosovo and Metohija and some from Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First there is a list of the secretariats on the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija and then some secretariats on the territory of Serbia. If I need to, I can tell you which ones they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we know which ones are not in Kosovo. Who else is the recipient of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The ministry staff in Pristina, the border police stations, do I need to read them all out?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell us whether they are all in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, they're not all in Kosovo. Prohor Pcinjski and Presevo are not in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who else is an addressee?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: The police administration as it says here, that means the headquarters of the ministry, the crime police administration, the traffic police administration, and the border police administration and OC, operations centre. These last five organizational units were in the ministry headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The dispatch we see before us, is it one that issues orders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a dispatch issuing orders as to certain measures to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in Kosovo and Metohija, who issued orders in full and directly to the units in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: It was the Ministry of the Interior, and most often it said public security sector in the heading or a subordinate administration if it referred strictly to one line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this document in accordance with what you say about this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because all the secretariats are listed as addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The line of issuing orders and reporting orders, meaning "nalog," while you were in Kosovo and Metohija as a member of the staff between the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior and the secretariats of the interior remain unchanged -- did it remain unchanged regardless of the existence of the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it remained intact, so the secretariats of the interior briefed the Ministry of the Interior directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And with regard to orders, "nalog"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: They arrived directly from the ministry, directly to the secretariats, and they were sent to the staff for information only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The fact that they were sent to the staff for information, was this done simultaneously, at the same time, as when the "nalog" was sent to the secretariats of the interior?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was done in parallel, as can be seen from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the secretariats of the interior automatically carried out the orders, the "nalog," that they received from the secretariat of the interior in Belgrade or the ministry?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they carried out these orders independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And whose orders did the lower organizational units of the Ministry of the Interior carry out in the public security sector? For example, the police stations and branch police stations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: When the secretariat of the interior received a certain order, "nalog," from the Ministry of the Interior, then it would issue the same "nalog" to its lower organizational units, such as the departments of the interior or the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the MUP staff have the ability to change something in an order arriving from the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, the MUP staff did not change these orders, these "nalog."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But did it have the power to change it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, because it did not issue them. So as you can see from this document, the ministry sending an order directly to the organizational units on the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us now what the line was how the regular tasks within the MUP were carried out.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Can show you this -- I can illustrate it by explaining the line of work I did. So when the border police administration issues a "nalog," an order, it is sent on to the secretariat of the interior, to the department carrying or the section carrying out those tasks. And then this department - I'm talking about my line of work now - these were territorial organizational units and they would have employees dealing with my line of work. And then my department would send the same order to them, we would forward the ministry order to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you say "my department," are you referring to when you were in the SUP or in the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to when I'm in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the MUP staff or its manager have the power to take disciplinary measures for failure to carry out tasks within the SUPs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no, no. The head of the staff or the Chief of Staff could not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a member of the staff, were you able to take measures linked to responsibility for failure to carry out tasks having to do with the departments and sectors for the border and foreign nationals?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the MUP staff or its head responsible to the minister for the work of the secretariat of the interior?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not responsible for the work of the secretariats, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you as a member of the staff responsible for the work of the departments and sectors within the SUPs, for foreign nationals and the border, or for the work of the border police stations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not responsible. As I have already stated, from the border police stations they were directly responsible to the administration and the sectors and departments were directly responsible to the Ministry of the Interior within which they were operating -- secretariat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not the ministry but the secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the MUP staff or its leader possessed of any authority as regards commendations, promotions, or dismissals of members of the organizational units of the Ministry of the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware that he had such powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have on e-court -- have 6D262.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've already seen this document in a different context. So now, in this particular context I'll ask you the following. Is this an example where from the public security sector the secretariats of the interior and the border police stations are being issued with direct orders -- I apologise, I misspoke, that the minister sends direct orders, "nalog," to the bodies I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an example of that because it says in the heading "Ministry of the Interior" and it doesn't say which organizational unit within the ministry is sending this document. And at the end of the document we see that it was signed by the minister, Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have in e-court document 6D267.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see the document. From which part of the ministry was this document sent?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the copy is barely legible, but I see it says "RJB," public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us who the signatory is?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Assistant to the minister, chief of the public security sector, Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell us the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not very clear here, but I think the date is the 3rd of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does this document refer to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: This document refers to the arrival of the Kosovo Verification Mission and it prescribes the obligations of police employees, where the mission would be located and how their status issues were to be regulated. And also, who was tasked with contacts with representatives of the verification mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 2, last paragraph, is the chief of the sector designating a person who is in charge of contacts with the KVM?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On behalf of the MUP staff in Pristina it was Colonel Miroslav Mijatovic, and in the headquarters of the secretariat the chiefs of the secretariats. And in other municipalities, the chiefs of the departments of the interior and the police station commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And does this dispatch have the nature of a "nalog"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this an example where a "nalog" is sent directly from the public security sector to the secretariats and the border police stations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because we see it was sent directly to the secretariats of the interior and to the border police stations, all of them -- all the ones, rather, on the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that one of the recipients is RDB. Was something issued to them as a "nalog," or was this for information only?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here that it was sent to them for information only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to clarify the everyday operations and work, I'll ask you about the SUPs first. Did the SUPs need any kind of "nalog" from the MUP staff to act on information, for example, that a crime had been committed or in connection with any other security-related event?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No. The secretariats, not only on the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, but throughout the territory of the Republic of Serbia were independent in their work. An annual and a monthly work-plan would be adopted, and they were duty-bound to act pursuant to those plans. Whenever a security-related event occurred such as a crime, the secretariats would act independently and they would inform the ministry of what action they had taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In connection with your line of work, did the ministry, or was the ministry staff supposed to regulate the functioning of the departments and sectors for the border and foreign nationals within the secretariat of the interior or was it supposed to regulate the work of the border police stations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No. I as a member of the staff dealing with that line of work did not do that, and I can explain why not. When I spoke about the administration of the border police, the administration had more than one organizational unit and these were also divided within that line of work according to the lines of work. And there were several persons able to monitor and control the work of the sectors and departments within the secretariat of the interior. I did not have the wherewithal to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say I did not have time and I could not do that, were you authorised to do something like that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 6D269 called up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While that's happening, can I just check one thing. Was there someone in the Pristina SUP office who dealt with the same sort of things as you dealt with in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the Pristina SUP there is also a border police department. If you allow me, I will explain. In the territory of the Republic of Serbia, in every secretariat there is an organizational unit that is involved in the kind of work that I was involved in. In larger secretariats, like the SUP of Nis, SUP of Pristina, SUP of Kragujevac, and SUP of Novi Sad, these organizational units are called departments. In smaller secretariats they are called divisions. While I was in Pristina, this department functioned absolutely normally and the department had its own head and had employees who were subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have before you 6D269?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of a document is this, please? Could you please tell us what kind of a document it is, who sent it, and when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. It was sent on the 18th of February, 1999. And in this document it is stated what should be done due to the complexity of the situation in the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in relation to the attacks by NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph is a fear expressed that there will be larger-scale movements of the population?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What is stated there, or rather, what is envisioned is that there may be larger-scale population movements from the border area further into the territory. I assume that the assessment was like that because an aggression was expected to be carried out by NATO forces, and it was expected that these forces would enter from the Republic of Macedonia and the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see anywhere in this document an assessment to the effect that the population might leave the country?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, I see no such assessment here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were in Kosovo only a few days into the bombing, but while you were still in Kosovo were you informed about documents being taken away from civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no one informed me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in Kosovo and later on, did you ever hear that anyone ordered that documents be taken away?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Also as far as I can remember, no one issued that kind of an order, "nalog," to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Seizing and destroying documents, would there be any point in that in terms of annulling citizens' status?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my view, seizing documents would be pointless. I can show this by resorting to the example of the personal identity card. For example, sometimes citizens used [as interpreted] their personal IDs. That doesn't mean that they no longer live where they live and it doesn't mean that they are not citizens of Serbia any longer. They lose their IDs, and that's it. For example, a photograph of a person to whom a personal ID is issued has that photograph both on the ID itself and also on a document that is kept in the file. Also, there is a finger-print of the right index finger. And then also as requests are received for issuing personal IDs, they are registered in certain logs and these logs are kept on a permanent basis. So we can always check to who a personal ID card was issued and when. In addition to that, there are ledgers with birth certificates and also books of citizens, nationals, and there are double copies at that. For example, if there is to be -- if there is a fire or any kind of accident, there is always another copy of that kind of birth register. So in my view, someone's existence cannot be simply annulled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, on page 78, line 3 [In English] We can see the word "used" should be "losed" so it's not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Lose, lose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's that somebody lost his ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I have a little request to make to clarify a position. Of course when documents are lost within a country and someone can approach the concern establishments for purposes of procuring its duplicates on the basis of proof, but what happens when somebody is to cross the border and he's gone; how will he come in without the documents? Can he get a duplicate in a foreign country? Now, that's a little clarification you'll have to add to what you have already said. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a citizen of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia loses his documents abroad, the duplicates of such documents cannot be issued to him. He is duty-bound to come to a diplomatic or a consular office of our country that issues him with a lesse passe in order to return to the country. So he is duty-bound to give truthful and accurate information about himself, and then these details are checked in the country. Of course say if this person says that he lives in Novi Sad, then the information is checked in Novi Sad, and then he gets a lesse passe in order to enter the country and then it is his duty to get duplicate documents in the country, he does it himself for all the documents that he had lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, page 78, line 16, I believe the witness says: In my view, someone's existence cannot be simply annulled by seizing the identification documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By seizing his documents, yeah. Thank you. Now, Mr. Lukic, is this a suitable time to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are aware of the situation, so we would rather have this witness finish if he wants to continue. We don't know what the position is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you would rather finish with Mr. Milenkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Mr. Vucurevic, we were in the middle of the evidence of Mr. Milenkovic when we brought you in. There was another issue to be dealt with. We're now in a position I think to return to his evidence, so we will interrupt your evidence at this stage, regrettably. Whatever we had done today, you are going to be back here on Monday in any event. However, meanwhile would you please leave the courtroom with the usher and stay in this building. I will speak to you again at some stage before you leave for the evening or possibly you may be back in the witness box continuing your evidence. At the moment the position is not clear, but we will speak to you a bit later on this afternoon. Now please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe you should warn this witness about contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thought maybe you should warn this witness about his duty not to contact anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that will be before he leaves -- he won't be leaving until later this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that following the request made by the Trial Chamber the Tribunal registry arranged for you to meet with Mr. Milenkovic to advise him of his rights in terms of Rule 90(E) of the Tribunal's Rules. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you confirm to us that you have fully advised him of his rights under the rule?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does he understand them?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you consider it necessary that you should remain here?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. By your leave, I should like to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give us one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milenkovic, are you satisfied that you have received appropriate advice of your rights under Rule 90(E) of the Tribunal's Rules from Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you now content to proceed to give further evidence in her absence? She may now leave the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am fully prepared to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are extremely grateful to you, Ms. Nikolic, for the assistance you've afforded at very short notice and you may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milenkovic, you will appreciate your entitlement to refuse to answer any question where you consider that the answer may incriminate you; should that situation arise, you should draw that to my attention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me if you consider you do not wish to answer a question. You understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand you and I'm going to reply to each and every one of your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, of course it should be made clear to you that you are also absolutely entitled to answer any question you wish to answer. Mr. Hannis, you may now continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milenkovic, I'd like to start by showing you a photograph that is Exhibit P2629. I can give you a hard copy. It will be on the screen as well. Now, I understand that you've seen this photograph before when you spoke with the war crimes prosecutor, and I believe that's Mr. Stankovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us that was in March of 2007. Did you not see this photograph prior to that date?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, I had never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't see the version that was in the media in the Danas article at the end of January 2007 which is the same picture except with a black bar over part of your face? You didn't see that one?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I read the newspapers very often but only sports newspapers. I heard of that picture that was published in the newspaper called Danas and I made quite a bit of effort in order to get a copy of that newspaper and I did see that picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime towards the end of January, something like that, roughly, I cannot give you the exact date, but I think it was after the 25th of January, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that was the first time you saw this photograph then, in January 2007?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I think that that would be right as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You realize that photograph was taken by one of your colleagues from the 37th Detachment of the PJP? Please don't name any name, but you're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who took this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time of that event there was nobody else within camera range to take such photograph, was there, other than your colleagues from the 37th?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: In that action that we took part in there were six of us taking part. So I really could not see or did I expect any one of us to have a camera on him and take pictures of what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned that when you met with the war crimes prosecutor he showed you five photographs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to show you two other photographs, Exhibit P2630, which is a picture of the wounded man that's in the one you currently have before you; and then P2628, which is of another individual. We'll look at 2630 first. That photograph of the man who's in the picture where you appear, is that another one of the photographs the war crimes prosecutor showed you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the third one of another wounded terrorist or KLA person, and it's 2629, I believe, is that another one that was shown to you by the prosecutor Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what the other two photographs were of?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I think it was one person who was on a blanket or on a -- or on a tarpaulin. I don't remember the rest because it was really over a year ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. P2628 is a picture of a person on a blanket. Did you see additional pictures of him?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see any other photograph. I'm not sure. That's the way it seems to be, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not clear now. I thought you told us you saw five photographs when you talked with Prosecutor Stankovic. Is that correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. I think that I was shown five photographs, but I'm not sure whether all five involved these persons or whether there was yet another photograph as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We had earlier evidence, Mr. Hannis, of the photograph of the men on and around the tank as being one of the photographs shown to him by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think he indicated that was not one of the five that he was shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's I think correct, just to ensure there's no confusion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, those other two photographs you -- are you saying they were of some different individuals than the two wounded KLA persons we see in those three that you have on the desk in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that they were only photographs that can be -- of the persons that can be seen here in these photographs that are in front of me. There was even one, I can't remember which one it was exactly, with the tank that you showed me before this break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. When you talked about this before, I understood that on this occasion you found only two living wounded KLA members or terrorists after that initial fighting which you said lasted about two hours, correct? There weren't any other living or surviving fighters in that location, were there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: In addition to these two wounded persons, there weren't any others there at that location except for those who had escaped into the forests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, apart from some that had fled beyond your reach, the only ones you had found were some dead ones and then these two that you captured, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go through the sequence with you again to be sure I understand. At page 22975, line 24, you said: "We combed the terrain crawling, trying to avoid being seen from the terrorists hiding in the vineyards, trying to avoid getting killed, and at one point we heard somebody moaning from inside a connecting trench." Is that right so far?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part you got it right, but the fire that was opened at us was the moment when we were crawling to this place where their connection trenches were, where they were fortified. Fire was opened from the thicket nearby, which we saw when a few of them escaped. As for the moans, we heard them, or rather, I heard it when I got close to the communication trench, when I crawled close to their trenches that had been dug before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I understood your answer yesterday you said: "We heard somebody moaning from inside a connecting trench." The moaning you heard was coming from a trench, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you went on to say that Dejan Mihajlovic and Zoran the commander were the first to go in, that you weren't far from there, and you heard from them there were people wounded inside. You then say: "I came out from behind a bush holding my rifle in the combat posture that I learned during training, and that's the posture you see on the photograph as I'm standing over this seriously wounded man who was gasping for breath and there came a wheezing sound from his throat so he was -- he was so badly wounded." Now, I took it from that description yesterday that that photograph of you standing over the man is when you came out from behind the bush, right, that's the first moment you came upon him, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that inside a trench? The photograph doesn't look like it's inside a trench that I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot answer that question, but I believe this is right next to that trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you told us that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we're going to have questions on a picture, I think we should have that picture up on the screen. I think we have the other picture up on the screen from my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, the witness has the picture in front of him I think, Mr. Hannis, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we should all see it on the screen. Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, now I need to move to another picture for the next question. You told us that this seriously wounded man had a throat wound, is that correct, or a neck wound? Didn't you tell us that the other day?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that's what I said. I said that he had blood on his face, but his wounds were to the arm and his knee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we look at the photograph P2630 right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where his arm wound was? I can see in general where the leg wound might be, but on this photograph I can't see an arm wound.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I have to show you if you want to look at me. His wound was here, in this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're pointing to the underside of your left bicep, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it wasn't so bad that he wasn't able to extend both of his arms up toward you where we saw in the earlier photograph where you're standing over him, right? Which is P2629 for the record. You see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The wound to his left arm was not so bad that he was not able to raise and extend both of his arms up toward you as you were standing over him, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: I only saw that he was wounded in the arm and bleeding from that wound. Now, how serious that wound was, I wasn't in a position to assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there was a tourniquet on his leg but there was no tourniquet on his arm wound, was there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you did not have your finger on the trigger. I would ask you to look again at that photograph. Isn't your index finger extended through the trigger housing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have the photograph on the screen then, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, P2629 should be on the screen now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you hear the question? Could you repeat it please, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there was a tourniquet on his leg but there was no tourniquet on his arm wound, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You asked that. It's the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your finger, your index finger, is extended through the trigger housing, is it not, on your right hand?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC
